When Sara came into the schoolroom the following morning, every girl watched her with wide, curious eyes. They had all heard plenty about her already, from Lavinia Herbert, almost thirteen and convinced she was quite grown up, down to four-year-old Lottie Legh, the school's baby. They knew without a doubt that Miss Minchin meant to show her off as a credit to the school. A girl or two had even glimpsed Mariette, her French maid, who had arrived the previous evening. Lavinia had contrived to walk past Sara's open door and catch sight of Mariette unpacking a box delivered late from one of the shops.

"It was packed with petticoats covered in lace frills—rows and rows of them," she whispered to her friend Jessie, bending over her geography book. "I watched her shake them out. Miss Minchin told Miss Amelia, and I heard her, that those clothes were so grand they were ridiculous for a child. My mamma says a child ought to dress simply. She's wearing one of those petticoats this minute. I caught sight of it as she sat down."
Jessie bent over her geography book too. "She's wearing silk stockings!" she whispered. "And such tiny feet! I've never seen feet so small."

Lavinia gave a spiteful sniff. "Oh, that's just how her slippers are shaped. My mamma says a clever shoemaker can make even large feet seem small. I don't find her pretty in the least. What a strange colour her eyes are."

"She isn't pretty in the usual sort of way," Jessie said, sneaking another look across the room. "But you feel like looking at her again. Her eyelashes are amazingly long, though her eyes are practically green."

In her place near Miss Minchin's desk, Sara waited quietly for instructions. All those watching eyes did not embarrass her in the least. Curious herself, she calmly returned the other children's looks. What, she wondered, were they thinking? Did they like Miss Minchin? Did they enjoy their lessons? And did any of them have a papa anything like hers? Earlier that morning she had talked to Emily about her father for a long time.

"Emily, he's out at sea now," she had told her. "You and I must be the very best of friends and tell one another everything. Look at me, Emily. No one has nicer eyes than yours—but how I wish you could talk."

Her head was full of imaginary worlds and curious ideas. One of these was that simply pretending Emily was alive, and could truly hear and understand, might be a great comfort. Mariette dressed her in a dark-blue frock for lessons and fastened a dark-blue ribbon in her hair. Then Sara went over to Emily, seated in a chair of her own, and handed her a book.
"Here's something to read while I'm downstairs," she told her. Noticing Mariette's curious gaze, she turned to explain, with a very serious little face.

"I think dolls can do all sorts of things they keep hidden from us," she said. "Perhaps Emily really knows how to read and speak and walk, but waits until everyone has left the room before she does any of it. It's her secret. After all, if people found out what dolls could do, they'd put them to work. Perhaps the dolls have all promised one another never to tell. While you're here, Emily will only sit and stare. Once you leave, though, she may start reading or walk over to look through the window. If she heard either of us coming back, she'd hurry to her chair, jump up into it, and make believe she'd been sitting there the whole time."

"Comme elle est drole!" Mariette thought, and later, downstairs, she repeated the story to the head housemaid. Already, though, she was growing fond of this unusual little girl, with her clever small face and faultless manners. Other children she had cared for had been far less courteous. Sara was a very fine little person. There was something delightful in the gentle gratitude with which she said, "If you please, Mariette," and "Thank you, Mariette." As Mariette explained to the head housemaid, the child thanked her exactly as she would thank a lady.
"Elle a l'air d'une princesse, cette petite," she said. In fact, her new little mistress pleased her very much indeed, and she was delighted with her position.
A few minutes passed while Sara sat under the other pupils' gaze. Then Miss Minchin gave a dignified tap on her desk to call for attention.

"Young ladies," she announced, "let me introduce your new companion." Every little girl stood beside her seat, and Sara got up too. "I expect you all to make yourselves most agreeable to Miss Crewe. She has travelled a very long way to join us—all the way from India, in fact. When lessons finish, you must get to know one another."
The other pupils made formal bows, and Sara answered with a small curtsy. Then everyone sat down and resumed looking at everyone else.
In her classroom voice, Miss Minchin said, "Sara, come over here to me."
She had lifted a book from her desk and was leafing through it. Sara approached with quiet courtesy.
"Since your papa has hired a French maid to attend you," she began, "I assume he wants you to pay particular attention to studying French."
Sara felt rather uncomfortable.
"I believe he chose her because he—he thought I would like her, Miss Minchin," she replied.

With a faintly sour smile, Miss Minchin said, "I'm afraid you have been a very spoiled little girl. You always suppose things are arranged simply to please you. I believe your papa's intention was for you to learn French."

Had Sara been a little older, or less determined to show perfect politeness to everyone, a few words would have settled the misunderstanding. Instead she felt her cheeks grow hot. Miss Minchin was stern and imposing. She seemed so completely certain that Sara knew no French at all that contradicting her felt almost impolite. In fact, Sara could remember no time when French had seemed unfamiliar. Her father had spoken it to her often, even when she was a baby. Her mother had been French, and Captain Crewe loved her language; so Sara had always heard it around her and had grown up knowing it.
"I—I haven't exactly studied French, but—but—" she started, making a timid effort to explain.

Not knowing how to speak French herself was one of Miss Minchin's most deeply irritating secrets, and she was anxious to keep it hidden. She had no wish to pursue the subject and risk innocent questions from a little pupil who had only just arrived.

"Enough," she replied, tart beneath her politeness. "If you have never learned it, you must start immediately. Monsieur Dufarge, our French master, is due in a few minutes. Take this book and study it while you wait for him."

Her cheeks burning, Sara returned to her place and opened the book. With a solemn face she examined its opening page. To smile would be rude, she knew, and she was determined to avoid rudeness. Yet how strange to be set to study a page explaining that "le pere" was "the father" and "la mere" was "the mother."
Miss Minchin gave her a searching look.
"Sara, you seem rather bad-tempered," she remarked. "I'm sorry that learning French is such an unwelcome prospect."
Deciding to make another attempt, Sara replied, "I like it very much indeed, but—"
"When someone tells you to do something, you mustn't answer 'but,'" Miss Minchin said. "Return your attention to the book."
Sara obeyed. She kept from smiling even at the information that "le fils" was "the son" and "le frere" was "the brother."
"Once Monsieur Dufarge gets here," she thought, "I'll be able to explain it to him."

Monsieur Dufarge appeared soon afterwards. A pleasant, intelligent Frenchman of middle age, he noticed Sara with interest as she made a courteous effort to look completely absorbed in the little phrase book.
"Have you a new pupil for me, madame?" he asked Miss Minchin. "I hope I am that fortunate."

Miss Minchin replied, "Her papa, Captain Crewe, is most eager for her to start learning the language. Unfortunately, she seems to have a childish dislike of it. I'm afraid she shows little willingness to learn."
Turning kindly to Sara, he said, "That makes me sorry, mademoiselle. Perhaps, once our lessons begin, I shall be able to show you how charming a language it is."

Little Sara stood up. She was growing quite desperate, with the feeling that she was almost in disgrace. Raising her large green-grey eyes to Monsieur Dufarge's face, she looked at him with innocent appeal. The moment she spoke, she knew, he would understand. In lovely, fluent French, she gave a simple explanation. Madame had misunderstood her. She had never exactly studied French—not from books—but her papa and other people had always used it when they spoke to her. She had read and written it just as she had English. Her papa loved the language, and she loved it for his sake. Her dear mamma, who had died at her birth, was French. She would gladly learn whatever monsieur cared to teach her. All she had meant to tell madame was that the words in this particular book were already familiar to her. As she said it, she offered him the little phrase book.

At Sara's first words Miss Minchin gave a violent start. She stared over her spectacles, looking almost offended, and went on staring until the explanation ended. Monsieur Dufarge, meanwhile, began to smile with unmistakable delight. That sweet child's voice, speaking his own tongue so naturally and charmingly, made him feel almost at home again. On London's dark, fog-bound days, his native country could seem worlds away. When Sara stopped speaking, he accepted the phrase book with a look bordering on affection. It was Miss Minchin, however, whom he addressed.
"Ah, madame," he said, "I can teach her very little. French is not something she has LEARNED; she is French herself. What an exquisite accent."
Deeply embarrassed, Miss Minchin turned on Sara. "You should have explained that to me," she exclaimed.
"I—I did try," Sara replied. "Perhaps I—I didn't begin in the proper way."

Miss Minchin knew perfectly well that Sara had tried. She knew, too, that the child was not to blame for being given no chance to explain. But the other pupils had been listening, and Lavinia and Jessie were laughing behind their French grammars. The sight filled her with fury.
She rapped sharply on the desk. "Silence, young ladies!" she commanded. "Be silent this instant!"
From that very moment, she began to bear a certain resentment towards her prize pupil.
